Reflecting on Personal Growth and Goals







Today, as I sit to pen down my thoughts, I find myself reflecting on the journey of personal growth and the goals that have shaped this path. It's been a year of profound learning, challenges, and self-discovery. I've come to appreciate the importance of small steps and the value of patience in the pursuit of larger ambitions.

Gratitude and Achievements

  • Personal Milestones:
  • Completed my first half-marathon, a testament to months of training and discipline.
  • Successfully led a project at work, enhancing my leadership skills and team collaboration.
  • Learning and Development:
  • Enrolled in a language course, embracing the beauty of cultural diversity and communication.
  • Dedicated time each week to reading, expanding my horizons and understanding on various subjects.

Challenges and Lessons

Life, as always, presented its fair share of challenges. Each hurdle brought with it valuable lessons:

  • Overcoming Procrastination:
    Discovered the power of the Pomodoro Technique, breaking tasks into manageable intervals, significantly boosting productivity.
  • Navigating Uncertainty:
  • Learned to embrace uncertainty, finding peace in the present moment and focusing on what I can control.

Goals for the Upcoming Months

  • Health and Wellness:
  • Aim to meditate daily, fostering mental clarity and emotional stability.
  • Incorporate yoga into my routine for better physical and mental balance.
  • Professional Growth:
  • Seek mentorship to navigate career aspirations and expand professional network.
  • Enhance my technical skills through online courses, focusing on data analysis and coding.

In Closing

As I look ahead, I'm filled with a sense of optimism and determination. The journey of personal growth is never linear, but each step, no matter how small, is a step forward. My goals are set, and my path is clear. Here's to embracing each moment, learning from each experience, and moving forward with gratitude and resilience.

This journal entry serves as a snapshot of personal reflections, challenges, and aspirations, utilizing various markdown features to organize and highlight key points. It's a blend of introspection and forward-looking goals, capturing the essence of personal growth and continuous learning.

In the realm of data analysis, leveraging MySQL queries is an indispensable technique for extracting valuable insights from databases. This Markdown note delves into the process of running analytics on a fictional "Users" and "Subscriptions" table, demonstrating how SQL queries can provide crucial information for decision-making.

The Database Structure

Let's assume a simplified database schema with two tables: "Users" and "Subscriptions."

  • Users Table:
  • Columns: user_id, username, email, registration_date, last_login
  • Subscriptions Table:
  • Columns: subscription_id, user_id, subscription_type, start_date, end_date, payment_status

Common Analytics Scenarios

1. Counting Users by Subscription Type

To gain an understanding of the distribution of subscription types among your users, you can use the following SQL query:

SELECT subscription_type, COUNT(*) as user_count
FROM Subscriptions
GROUP BY subscription_type;

2. Tracking Subscription Renewals

To monitor the renewal rate of subscriptions, you can identify how many subscriptions were renewed within a specified timeframe:

SELECT COUNT(*) as renewed_subscriptions
FROM Subscriptions
WHERE end_date >= CURDATE();

3. User Activity Analysis

By examining user login patterns, you can assess user engagement:

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(last_login, '%Y-%m-%d') as login_date, COUNT(*) as login_count
FROM Users
GROUP BY login_date
ORDER BY login_date;

4. Churn Rate Calculation

Determine the churn rate by analyzing users who have canceled their subscriptions:

SELECT COUNT(*) as churned_users
FROM Users
WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM Subscriptions WHERE end_date >= CURDATE());

5. Subscription Revenue

Calculate revenue generated from subscriptions:

SELECT SUM(payment_status) as total_revenue
FROM Subscriptions
WHERE payment_status = 'paid';

Advanced Analytics

MySQL queries offer even more powerful capabilities, such as joining tables, using subqueries, and applying advanced statistical functions. These capabilities enable you to conduct in-depth analysis, discover trends, and make data-driven decisions.

Whether you're exploring user behavior, tracking subscription performance, or deriving financial insights, MySQL queries are your trusty companions in extracting meaningful analytics from your database.

Marketing analytics is an indispensable tool for optimizing your website's performance and driving business growth. In the digital age, understanding how your online marketing efforts are faring is crucial. This Markdown note will explore various aspects of marketing analytics, including:

The Importance of Marketing Analytics

Marketing analytics provides actionable insights into your website's performance, helping you make informed decisions. It empowers you to track, measure, and evaluate various aspects of your online marketing campaigns. Some key benefits include:

  • Data-Driven Decisions: Marketing analytics allows you to base your decisions on concrete data, not guesswork.
  • ROI Assessment: You can calculate the return on investment (ROI) for different marketing channels and campaigns.
  • Audience Insights: Understand your audience's behavior, preferences, and demographics to tailor your strategies accordingly.

Key Metrics to Track

To effectively analyze your website's performance, monitor these essential metrics:

Metric

Description

Traffic Sources

Identify where your website visitors are coming from.

Conversion Rate

Measure the percentage of visitors who take desired actions.

Bounce Rate

Assess the rate at which users leave your site without interacting.

Click-Through Rate (CTR)

Evaluate the effectiveness of your calls to action.

Tools for Marketing Analytics

Several tools and platforms can aid in marketing analytics, such as:

  1. Google Analytics: A comprehensive tool for tracking website performance and user behavior.
  1. HubSpot: Offers marketing analytics along with customer relationship management (CRM) capabilities.
  1. Adobe Analytics: Provides robust analytics solutions for in-depth data analysis.

Implementing Marketing Analytics

To get started with marketing analytics, follow these steps:

  1. Set Objectives: Define clear goals and objectives for your website and marketing campaigns.
  1. Choose Metrics: Select relevant metrics based on your objectives.
  1. Integrate Tools: Implement analytics tools like Google Analytics on your website.
  1. Regular Analysis: Continuously monitor and analyze data to identify trends and areas for improvement.

Conclusion

In the world of online marketing, understanding the performance of your website is vital. Marketing analytics equips you with the insights needed to make informed decisions and optimize your digital marketing efforts. By tracking key metrics and using appropriate tools, you can achieve greater success in your online endeavors.

title: The Unexpected Benefits of Encrypted Writing

content.data:
Let's admit, shall we, that freedom has to have its own space.

I've spent more than the last decade of my life developing tools for note taking, the most important of which is an encrypted note-taking app. And when I talk to users about how their lives changed once they knew their thoughts and words were private, the response is always the same: "I feel free," is what I hear. They talk about the subtle but powerful difference privacy brings you. You become accustomed to the luxury of knowing what you say will never be repeated.

Those who haven't tried the private online life ask me what it's like.

Imagine you are in a room with fifty people. It's crowded. The air is muddled and warmer than comfortable. Your thoughts and very mode of being are altered by the environment. You are distracted. You are influenced by what you hear. You don't have the same thoughts you'd have if you were alone.

Now imagine that every thing you said in that room in a private conversation had a chance of being heard or recorded by someone else. Life changes. Suddenly you worry what you said. What you might say. You are a whole different person. You become a subdued version of yourself, limited in your creativity and oomph.

Internet living is about being in a room with hundreds of millions of people. We are not ourselves here. We have to be cautious and adapt to where we are. We find ourselves multiplying. We are a hundred different people, depending where on the web we are that day. I know that when I speak with friends on Slack, or write a note on Evernote or Google Docs, there is an ever-present chance that what I am typing will one day be seen by someone else beyond the intended audience. And with this thought lingering, I do not write like I would in a private journal. I write as if an audience were present. I pause between sentences to look both ways.

I write as if to say, "If this got out, how would it make me look? What would others think of me?" And in that way, my writing loses its most important part: Me.

That's why I spend the time on encryption and privacy. I don't want the worry and hassle of others watching me. I don't want to have to check my doors every night. I want to know I am safe to be me. To have my best thoughts. To write without worry of perfection.

I just want to write like it's nobody's business.

title: Don't be fooled_ Metadata is the real data

content.data:
In a crime case, investigators don't have access to "the truth"—the data, if you will. All they have are clues which can be put together to make as perfect a guess as possible as to what the nature of the truth is. Metadata.

In the U.S, governments have played coy and attempted to talk down efforts of mass surveillance, particularly phone surveillance, by asserting that the actual contents of the call are not collected—only the metadata is:

  • Where you were
  • Who you were calling
  • How long you talked for
  • How frequently you talk to someone

In a crime investigation, having the answers to these kinds of questions could potentially make or break a case.

And that's precisely why governments collect this kind of information: it is powerful fodder in a legal setting. In an example most of us are probably familiar with, you can see that who Adnan Syed called and when were some of the most important deciding factors in placing him in a jail cell.

And as it can be used for legal justice in some cases, or the "good", it can also be used against you, like you're warned of in your Miranda rights.

So what do we do?

We protect ourselves and the people we care about, not against the government, but the possibility of government. We don't speak unless we have an attorney present. We plead the fifth.

We encrypt our data.

Smarter people before us have understood the unstoppable nature of government power, and have put in provisions such as separations of power and the Miranda rights precisely for this reason.

And today, smart people advocate endlessly for the encryption of your data as a form of self-protection. With anti-privacy legislation being signed today with a flick of a pen, it's more important than ever to understand that even metadata can and will be used against you. And, in the court of law, even if you have nothing to hide, or are fully innocent, you are still advised and even required to have a lawyer present before you can testify. Why? Because history.

Legal waters are not somewhere you want to swim in alone.

So the next time you hear that it's only "metadata" being collected, don't be fooled: metadata is the data.

This isn't to say that you shouldn't use apps that record metadata. Metadata is what allows a lot of your favorite apps to organize and keep your data in sync.

It's to instead say you should find no comfort in the fact that governments rely on the "metadata" crutch to make you feel ok with what they're doing.

The Bill of Rights of the United States constitution is about personal protections. These being such a fundamental part of our constitution is no coincidence: these were real dangers at some point.

  • The right to free speech
  • The right to bear arms
  • The right to remain silent

In today's world, we are the forefathers of a new constitution, a new amendment:

The right to encrypt.

It won't come easy, but then again, nothing important ever does.

# Code from http://sandbox.mc.edu/~bennet/ruby/code/poly_rb.html
#
# This program evaluates polynomials.  It first asks for the coefficients
# of a polynomial, which must be entered on one line, highest-order first.
# It then requests values of x and will compute the value of the poly for
# each x.  It will repeatly ask for x values, unless you the user enters
# a blank line.  It that case, it will ask for another polynomial.  If the
# user types quit for either input, the program immediately exits.
#

#
# Function to evaluate a polynomial at x.  The polynomial is given
# as a list of coefficients, from the greatest to the least.
def polyval(x, coef)
    sum = 0
    coef = coef.clone           # Don't want to destroy the original
    while true
        sum += coef.shift       # Add and remove the next coef
        break if coef.empty?    # If no more, done entirely.
        sum *= x                # This happens the right number of times.
    end
    return sum
end

#
# Function to read a line containing a list of integers and return
# them as an array of integers.  If the string conversion fails, it
# throws TypeError.  If the input line is the word 'quit', then it
# converts it to an end-of-file exception
def readints(prompt)
    # Read a line
    print prompt
    line = readline.chomp
    raise EOFError.new if line == 'quit' # You can also use a real EOF.
            
    # Go through each item on the line, converting each one and adding it
    # to retval.
    retval = [ ]
    for str in line.split(/\s+/)
        if str =~ /^\-?\d+$/
            retval.push(str.to_i)
        else
            raise TypeError.new
        end
    end

    return retval
end

#
# Take a coeff and an exponent and return the string representation, ignoring
# the sign of the coefficient.
def term_to_str(coef, exp)
    ret = ""

    # Show coeff, unless it's 1 or at the right
    coef = coef.abs
    ret = coef.to_s     unless coef == 1 && exp > 0
    ret += "x" if exp > 0                               # x if exponent not 0
    ret += "^" + exp.to_s if exp > 1                    # ^exponent, if > 1.

    return ret
end

#
# Create a string of the polynomial in sort-of-readable form.
def polystr(p)
    # Get the exponent of first coefficient, plus 1.
    exp = p.length

    # Assign exponents to each term, making pairs of coeff and exponent,
    # Then get rid of the zero terms.
    p = (p.map { |c| exp -= 1; [ c, exp ] }).select { |p| p[0] != 0 }

    # If there's nothing left, it's a zero
    return "0" if p.empty?

    # *** Now p is a non-empty list of [ coef, exponent ] pairs. ***

    # Convert the first term, preceded by a "-" if it's negative.
    result = (if p[0][0] < 0 then "-" else "" end) + term_to_str(*p[0])

    # Convert the rest of the terms, in each case adding the appropriate
    # + or - separating them.  
    for term in p[1...p.length]
        # Add the separator then the rep. of the term.
        result += (if term[0] < 0 then " - " else " + " end) + 
                term_to_str(*term)
    end

    return result
end
        
#
# Run until some kind of endfile.
begin
    # Repeat until an exception or quit gets us out.
    while true
        # Read a poly until it works.  An EOF will except out of the
        # program.
        print "\n"
        begin
            poly = readints("Enter a polynomial coefficients: ")
        rescue TypeError
            print "Try again.\n"
            retry
        end
        break if poly.empty?

        # Read and evaluate x values until the user types a blank line.
        # Again, an EOF will except out of the pgm.
        while true
            # Request an integer.
            print "Enter x value or blank line: "
            x = readline.chomp
            break if x == ''
            raise EOFError.new if x == 'quit'

            # If it looks bad, let's try again.
            if x !~ /^\-?\d+$/
                print "That doesn't look like an integer.  Please try again.\n"
                next
            end

            # Convert to an integer and print the result.
            x = x.to_i
            print "p(x) = ", polystr(poly), "\n"
            print "p(", x, ") = ", polyval(x, poly), "\n"
        end
    end
rescue EOFError
    print "\n=== EOF ===\n"
rescue Interrupt, SignalException
    print "\n=== Interrupted ===\n"
else
    print "--- Bye ---\n"
end

This is another recipe we saw on Jamie Oliver’s TV show, and we can’t stop making it. It’s perfect for parties, and pairs well with any rich dip (we’ve been doing greek yogurt topped with hot sauce and tahini). We’ve also rolled things other than carrots, changed the flavors, made news dips— go wild!

Ingredients

  • 1 lb carrot sticks (or baby carrots)
  • 2 oranges (or any citrus)
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 1 package phyllo dough
  • 1/2 cup honey
  • sesame seeds to top
  • vegetable oil


Directions

  • Start by parboiling your carrots in 2 cups of water (means party boil).
  • Zest and juice the oranges.
  • When the carrots are jussst soft, drain the water. Add the butter, the zest, and the orange juice. Simmer until thick and delicious. It’s fine (and good) if the carrots are still a bit undercooked (we’re going to bake them next).
  • Unroll the phyllo dough and cut it into three equal sections. With a brush, oil the top of each sheet.
  • Roll a carrot with a single section of phyllow dough, place on a baking sheet. Repeat and repeat and repeat.
  • When a full baking sheet is ready, brush the top of each roll with a little oil. Don’t worry about placing them too far about, they won’t raise much (at all).
  • Bake according to your phyllo dough box.
  • With 5 minutes left, brush the top of each roll with honey, then sprinkle with sesame seeds.

title: A brief guide to encryption in Standard Notes

content.data:
Because your time is short, we're going to breeze through this:

When you use Standard Notes with an account:

  • Your data is automatically end-to-end encrypted with your account master key. Your account master key is derived from your password. Your account master key and password never ever leave your device, and are never sent to our servers. Thus, no one but you can read your notes. Not us, not hackers, and not states.
  • Using the desktop and mobile app, your account master key is stored securely in your device's native keychain.
  • Using the web app, your account master key is stored plainly in local storage. (Keep reading for how to improve this.)

When you add an application passcode to an app that is signed into an account:

  • Your passcode is used to generate a "wrapping key". This key is never stored anywhere nor sent externally, but only exists temporarily in memory to perform an action (such as unlocking the application and decrypting your account keys).
  • Your account master key is encrypted with the passcode wrapping key, and the "wrapped" master key is stored in the app's local storage. This is more ideal than storing the master key plainly in the keychain.
  • This same mechanism applies to using the web app: when you add a passcode to a web app signed into your account, the account master key is now encrypted with the passcode wrapping key, and the wrapped master key is stored in local storage. This means that with a passcode, you can gain desktop-level security using the web app when it comes to key storage.

👉 More detailed reading here: https://standardnotes.com/help/79/how-does-standard-notes-encrypt-data-on-my-device

title: Is it safe to put passwords in Standard Notes_

content.data:
Standard Notes uses stronger encryption technology than industry-leading password managers. In most cases, leading password managers use PBKDF2 for key derivation and AES-256 for encryption. Standard Notes uses post-PBKDF2 Argon2 for key derivation and post-AES XChaCha20-Poly1305 for encryption. This means that Standard Notes makes for an excellent place to store passwords, keys, and other secretive credentials.

In addition, two-factor authentication enabled on your account can lead to even higher levels of security than offered by typical password managers.

Read more: https://standardnotes.com/help/34/can-i-store-passwords-in-standard-notes

import numpy as np
cimport cython
from libc.math cimport sqrt

@cython.boundscheck(False)
@cython.wraparound(False)
def pairwise_cython(double[:, ::1] X):
    cdef int M = X.shape[0]
    cdef int N = X.shape[1]
    cdef double tmp, d
    cdef double[:, ::1] D = np.empty((M, M), dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(M):
        for j in range(M):
            d = 0.0
            for k in range(N):
                tmp = X[i, k] - X[j, k]
                d += tmp * tmp
            D[i, j] = sqrt(d)
    return np.asarray(D)
